findings.title: Race condition in seat-map.json atomic write
findings.explanation: The atomic write pattern (write to tmp, then rename) is correct, but the lock is released BEFORE the rename operation. If another process acquires the lock immediately after releaseLock() but before renameSync(), it could read an inconsistent state of seat-map.json. This violates the atomicity guarantee of the write operation.
findings.fix: Move the releaseLock() call AFTER the fs.renameSync() operation to ensure the lock is held during the entire atomic write sequence.

findings.title: Port collision risk due to incorrect static port filtering
findings.code: const staticPtyPorts = Array.from(usedPorts).filter(p => p < 10000); // Assuming static ports are below 10000
findings.explanation: The code assumes all ports below 10000 are static and should be treated as a separate range. However, seat-map.json shows dynamically allocated ports (e.g., 9306 for seat-17) that are below 10000. This causes the port finder to incorrectly treat dynamic ports as static, leading to potential port collisions when allocating new seats.
findings.fix: Remove the static/dynamic port distinction entirely. Use the entire usedPorts set for collision detection without any range-based filtering.

findings.title: VS Code port allocation ignores PTY port collision
findings.explanation: The VS Code port allocation uses the same usedPorts set as the PTY port allocation, but the PTY port is added to usedPorts AFTER the VS Code port search begins. This creates a race condition where the VS Code port could be assigned the same value as the PTY port that was just allocated.
findings.fix: Move the usedPorts.add(ptyPort) call BEFORE the VS Code port allocation to ensure the PTY port is reserved before searching for the VS Code port.

findings.title: Inconsistent port range assumptions
findings.explanation: The code assumes PTY ports start at 9300, but seat-map.json shows PTY ports at 9301 and 9302. While this works, it creates a magic number dependency that could cause issues if the port range assumptions change. The hardcoded 9300 should be derived from the actual minimum PTY port in use.
findings.fix: Replace 9300 with Math.min(...staticPtyPorts.filter(p => p >= 9000)) to dynamically determine the minimum PTY port range.

findings.title: Lock file cleanup race during spawn failure
findings.explanation: During spawn failure cleanup, the lock file is released unconditionally. If multiple processes are trying to spawn simultaneously, this could lead to a race where Process A releases the lock, Process B acquires it, then Process A's cleanup deletes Process B's lock, breaking the locking mechanism.
findings.fix: Only release the lock in the failure cleanup if the current process actually holds it (check the PID in the lock file matches process.pid).

findings.code: usedPorts.add(ptyPort); // Claim it immediately so vsCodePort doesn't reuse it
findings.explanation: NOT A BUG. The port reservation is correctly handled by adding the PTY port to usedPorts before searching for the VS Code port. This prevents collision and is the correct pattern.

findings.title: Log file descriptor not closed on successful spawn
findings.explanation: logFd opened at line 164 but only closed in finally block after spawn (line ~220). On successful spawn, child.unref() called but logFd remains open indefinitely since finally executes after unref but process continues running. Open FDs accumulate with each spawn, exhausting system limits and causing future spawns to fail with EMFILE.
findings.fix: Move fs.closeSync(logFd) immediately after child.unref() in success path, before console.log success message.

findings.title: Lock acquisition race in spawn error undo loop
findings.explanation: Undo loop uses same busy-wait acquireLock logic without calling acquireLock() function. If lock file exists (another process holds it), enters infinite tight CPU spin loop: `while (Date.now() < endSleep) {}` with 100ms sleep. No timeout or exponential backoff. Will hang forever or thrash CPU if contention during cleanup window.
findings.fix: Extract undo logic into async function that calls acquireLock() properly. Add max retry limit with exponential backoff.

findings.title: Port exhaustion guaranteed by conflicting port ranges
findings.explanation: PTY ports calculated from ports <10000, VSCode ports also from ports <10000. seat-map.json shows existing seats using 9223-9224,9301-9306. After ~20 spawns, highestUsedPtyPort and highestUsedVsCodePort converge to same value. findFreePort() scans same exhausted range twice, but works (just inefficient). No crash but port scan becomes O(n²) slow.
findings.fix: Use separate port ranges: PTY >10000, VSCode 8000-9000. Or scan all used ports once.

findings.title: fetch polyfill before dotenv breaks .env loading
findings.explanation: fetch polyfill executes before require('dotenv').config(). node-fetch modifies global environment in way that interferes with dotenv parsing (seen in Node 16-18). PT_SHARED_SECRET etc. become undefined even when .env exists. Key fallback to send-pt-welcome.js parsing works around it.
findings.fix: Move dotenv.config() before fetch polyfill.

findings.explanation: seat-1, seat-2, seat-3, seat-4, seat-5, seat-6, seat-7, and seat-16 all claim port 9223.  city-spawn-claude.js uses findFreePort() to avoid re-use, but it only consults the dynamic algorithm when spawning; the static map is never validated for duplicates. findings.title: Unchecked fs.renameSync() can silently fail on Windows
findings.explanation: On Windows renameSync throws if the target is open by another process (common with aggressive AV or editors).  The error is not caught, so the seat map stays in tmp state and the next locker sees corrupted JSON, breaking all future spawns.
findings.fix: Wrap in try/catch, retry a few times with exponential back-off, or use fs.copyFileSync + fs.unlinkSync as fallback.

findings.title: Deadlock window during spawn failure rollback
findings.explanation: If the original lock file still exists (PID alive), the rollback loop spins hot for 15 s doing CPU-bound sleep, blocking the exit path.  This is not lethal but wastes an entire core and delays agent recovery.
findings.fix: Use setTimeout inside async function instead of the blocking sleep loop.

findings.title: Incorrect port reuse assumption in findFreePort
findings.explanation: The logic assumes that all used ports below 10000 are 'static' and should be excluded from dynamic port allocation. However, there is no guarantee that dynamically allocated ports (like `ptyPort` or `vsCodePort`) won't overlap with this range, potentially leading to a collision when `findFreePort` is called again for `vsCodePort`. This could cause port exhaustion or conflict if a dynamically allocated port is reused in the filtered set.
findings.fix: Explicitly track and exclude `ptyPort` and `vsCodePort` in the `usedPorts` set before determining the ranges for new ports to avoid overlap.

findings.title: Unnecessary log file creation before spawn validation
findings.explanation: The log file descriptor is created before the child process is validated to spawn successfully. If the spawn fails and the process exits, the log file descriptor is closed, but the file is still created unnecessarily. This is wasteful but does not break functionality.
findings.fix: Delay creating the log file descriptor until after the child process is confirmed to spawn successfully.

findings.title: Undefined behavior on invalid seatMap structure
findings.explanation: If `seatMap` is not an object or is null, a default empty structure is used. However, the subsequent logic assumes `seatMap.seats` and `seatMap.aliases` exist and are objects. If the input `seatMap` JSON is malformed or partially corrupted (e.g., missing required keys), this could lead to runtime errors when attempting to iterate over or modify non-existent properties. This breaks the seat map update process.
findings.fix: Validate the full structure of `seatMap` (including `seats` and `aliases` being non-null objects) before proceeding with dynamic updates. Provide a clear fallback or error handling for unexpected structures.

findings.title: Redundant error logging in main health check
findings.explanation: If the `fetch` call to the host endpoint fails, the error is logged, but the script immediately exits with `process.exit(1)`. While not breaking, this is redundant because the script will terminate without further action. A single clear exit message would suffice.
findings.fix: Remove the redundant error log and let the exit code indicate failure.

findings.fix: Replace the busy-wait with an asynchronous delay using setTimeout to avoid blocking the event loop, e.g., await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));

The catch block attempts to parse the error as JSON and then creates a default seatMap, but the readFile error will not be JSON. The catch block's error handling incorrectly assumes the error is from JSON.parse.

findings.title: Port collision due to reused port calculation
findings.code: const staticPtyPorts = Array.from(usedPorts).filter(p => p < 10000); // Assuming static ports are below 10000
findings.explanation: The usedPorts set includes both pty_port and port values from all seats. The code filters for ports < 10000 to find 'static' ports, but this assumption is arbitrary. In seat-map.json, seat-16 and seat-17 have pty_port values 9302 and 9306 (both < 10000) and are dynamically spawned seats, not static. This will cause the 'highestUsedPtyPort' calculation to incorrectly include these dynamic ports, potentially causing the findFreePort to start scanning from a port already in use by a dynamic seat, leading to a port collision.
findings.fix: Do not filter by port number. Instead, track used ports correctly and let findFreePort scan from a safe start (e.g., 9300). Or, distinguish static vs dynamic seats by a property (e.g., 'static': true).

findings.title: Inefficient lock acquisition loop
findings.explanation: The acquireLock function uses a busy-wait loop with a non-blocking setTimeout. This is inefficient and can cause high CPU usage if lock contention is high. It also does not handle the case where the lock file is removed between the stat check and the write attempt, potentially leading to unnecessary retries.
findings.fix: Use a proper locking library (like 'proper-lockfile') or implement exponential backoff with file watching.

findings.title: Race condition in stale lock cleanup
findings.explanation: If two processes simultaneously detect a stale lock (same PID not running), both may attempt to delete the lock file. One may succeed, then the other may also call unlinkSync, which will throw ENOENT (ignored by the outer catch). However, the first process may then immediately create a new lock, while the second process continues its loop and might also create a lock, leading to two locks being held.
findings.fix: After deleting the stale lock, immediately try to acquire the lock (write with 'wx') instead of continuing the loop. Or use atomic operations (rename) for lock acquisition.

findings.title: Undo logic can deadlock
findings.explanation: If the child process fails to spawn, the error handler attempts to re-acquire the lock to undo seat map changes. This uses a busy-wait loop that blocks the event loop (due to empty while loop). If another process holds the lock, this will spin for up to 15 seconds, blocking all other operations and potentially causing a deadlock if the other process is also waiting.
findings.fix: Use asynchronous polling with setTimeout or implement a proper locking mechanism with retries that yields the event loop.

findings.title: Hardcoded path for log directory
findings.explanation: The log directory is assumed to be one level up from the script's location. If the script is run from a different working directory or the project structure changes, this path may be incorrect, leading to failed log file creation.

findings.explanation: If the log file cannot be opened (e.g., permissions, disk full), openSync will throw an unhandled exception, crashing the script. The error is not caught, which could leave the seat-map locked.

After ~20 spawns, highestUsedPtyPort and highestUsedVsCodePort converge to same value. findFreePort() scans same exhausted range twice, but works (just inefficient). No crash but port scan becomes O(n²) slow.
allFindings.fix: Use separate port ranges: PTY >10000, VSCode 8000-9000. Or scan all used ports once.

allFindings.title: Hardcoded port range assumption
allFindings.explanation: The code assumes static ports are below 10000, which might not be the case if seat-map.json is configured differently. This assumption can lead to incorrect port allocation.
allFindings.fix: Update the logic to dynamically check the current configuration instead of assuming a static range.

allFindings.title: Incorrect port reuse assumption in findFreePort
allFindings.explanation: The logic assumes that all used ports below 10000 are 'static' and should be excluded from dynamic port allocation. However, there is no guarantee that dynamically allocated ports (like `ptyPort` or `vsCodePort`) won't overlap with this range, potentially leading to a collision when `findFreePort` is called again for `vsCodePort`. This could cause port exhaustion or conflict if a dynamically allocated port is reused in the filtered set.
allFindings.fix: Explicitly track and exclude `ptyPort` and `vsCodePort` in the `usedPorts` set before determining the ranges for new ports to avoid overlap.

allFindings.title: Port collision due to reused port calculation
allFindings.code: const staticPtyPorts = Array.from(usedPorts).filter(p => p < 10000); // Assuming static ports are below 10000
allFindings.explanation: The usedPorts set includes both pty_port and port values from all seats. The code filters for ports < 10000 to find 'static' ports, but this assumption is arbitrary. In seat-map.json, seat-16 and seat-17 have pty_port values 9302 and 9306 (both < 10000) and are dynamically spawned seats, not static. This will cause the 'highestUsedPtyPort' calculation to incorrectly include these dynamic ports, potentially causing the findFreePort to start scanning from a port already in use by a dynamic seat, leading to a port collision.
allFindings.fix: Do not filter by port number. Instead, track used ports correctly and let findFreePort scan from a safe start (e.g., 9300). Or, distinguish static vs dynamic seats by a property (e.g., 'static': true).

allFindings.title: Hardcoded path for log directory
allFindings.explanation: The log directory is assumed to be one level up from the script's location. If the script is run from a different working directory or the project structure changes, this path may be incorrect, leading to failed log file creation.
allFindings.fix: Use a configurable environment variable or a project root-relative path that is verified.

allFindings.title: VS Code port search starts incorrectly due to commingled port sets
allFindings.explanation: The code uses the same usedPorts set (which contains both pty_port and port values) to compute the start port for VS Code port search. Since pty_port values (e.g., 9306) are higher, the search may start at an unnecessarily high port (e.g., 9307), skipping lower available ports (e.g., 9225). This is inefficient but does not cause functional failure.
allFindings.fix: Separate used ports by type: collect only seat.port values (excluding null) for VS Code port start calculation, and only seat.pty_port values for PTY port start calculation.

allFindings.title: Port exhaustion risk due to overlapping port ranges
allFindings.explanation: The code calculates the highest used PTY port by taking the maximum of 9300, all static PTY ports (assumed to be below 10000), and 0. This approach assumes that ports below 10000 are reserved for static seats, but it doesn't account for all dynamic allocations. If dynamic ports are also below 10000, this could lead to port exhaustion.
allFindings.fix: Refine the port discovery logic to dynamically determine the range of ports reserved for static allocations and ensure dynamic allocations do not overlap with this range. Consider maintaining a separate configuration for reserved port ranges.

representative.title: Busy-wait loop blocks event loop during undo operation
representative.explanation: The busy-wait loop synchronously blocks the Node.js event loop for up to 100ms per iteration during seat-map undo on spawn failure, causing potential delays in other operations and inefficiency. If the lock cannot be acquired, undo may fail, leaving orphan seat entries in seat-map.json, but this does not cause crashes or data loss as the system can still function with manual cleanup.
representative.fix: Replace the busy-wait with an asynchronous delay using setTimeout to avoid blocking the event loop, e.g., await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 100));

It also does not handle the case where the lock file is removed between the stat check and the write attempt, potentially leading to unnecessary retries.
allFindings.fix: Use a proper locking library (like 'proper-lockfile') or implement exponential backoff with file watching.

allFindings.title: Undo logic can deadlock
allFindings.explanation: If the child process fails to spawn, the error handler attempts to re-acquire the lock to undo seat map changes. This uses a busy-wait loop that blocks the event loop (due to empty while loop). If another process holds the lock, this will spin for up to 15 seconds, blocking all other operations and potentially causing a deadlock if the other process is also waiting.
allFindings.fix: Use asynchronous polling with setTimeout or implement a proper locking mechanism with retries that yields the event loop.

allFindings.title: Inconsistent lock acquisition in spawn failure cleanup
allFindings.explanation: When child process fails to spawn, the cleanup code attempts to re-acquire the lock using a custom busy-wait loop instead of calling the established acquireLock() function. This bypasses the robust lock validation (stale PID check, timeout logic) and could lead to deadlock or race conditions if another process holds the lock. It also uses a blocking sleep (busy loop), which is inefficient and can cause high CPU usage.
allFindings.fix: Replace the custom lock acquisition with a call to acquireLock() (or a helper that uses the same logic) and ensure proper release.

If multiple processes are trying to spawn simultaneously, this could lead to a race where Process A releases the lock, Process B acquires it, then Process A's cleanup deletes Process B's lock, breaking the locking mechanism.
representative.fix: Only release the lock in the failure cleanup if the current process actually holds it (check the PID in the lock file matches process.pid).

allFindings.fix: Use setTimeout inside async function instead of the blocking sleep loop.

allFindings.explanation: The code does not handle the case where the seat-map.json file is deleted or becomes inaccessible after the lock is acquired. This can lead to a deadlock where the lock is held indefinitely, preventing other processes from acquiring the lock and modifying the seat-map.
allFindings.fix: Add a check to verify the file exists and is readable after acquiring the lock. If the file is missing or unreadable, the function should throw an error or handle it gracefully to prevent deadlocks. For example, add a fs.statSync call after acquiring the lock to ensure the file is still valid.

allFindings.title: Potential race condition in lock release
allFindings.explanation: The `releaseLock` function attempts to delete the lock file but does not handle errors other than silently catching them. If the lock file is not deleted due to a permission issue or if another process has already deleted it, this could lead to a race condition where the lock is not properly released.
allFindings.fix: Add error logging for `fs.unlinkSync` to detect and handle failures when attempting to release the lock. Consider using `fs.unlink` with error handling to ensure proper cleanup.

representative.title: Race condition in seat-map.json atomic write
representative.explanation: The atomic write pattern (write to tmp, then rename) is correct, but the lock is released BEFORE the rename operation. If another process acquires the lock immediately after releaseLock() but before renameSync(), it could read an inconsistent state of seat-map.json. This violates the atomicity guarantee of the write operation.
representative.fix: Move the releaseLock() call AFTER the fs.renameSync() operation to ensure the lock is held during the entire atomic write sequence.

allFindings.title: Unchecked fs.renameSync() can silently fail on Windows
allFindings.explanation: On Windows renameSync throws if the target is open by another process (common with aggressive AV or editors).  The error is not caught, so the seat map stays in tmp state and the next locker sees corrupted JSON, breaking all future spawns.
allFindings.fix: Wrap in try/catch, retry a few times with exponential back-off, or use fs.copyFileSync + fs.unlinkSync as fallback.

allFindings.title: Race condition on seat ID allocation after port scan
allFindings.explanation: The nextSeatId is determined before ports are allocated, but if two instances run concurrently, both could calculate the same maxSeatNum from the same seat-map state and assign the same nextSeatId. Although file locking is used, the lock is released and reacquired during spawn failure cleanup without re-reading the seat-map, risking duplicate seat IDs.
allFindings.fix: Ensure seat ID incrementation and port assignment occur atomically under lock, and re-validate seat-map state before writing if reacquiring lock after spawn failure.

representative.fix: Move fs.closeSync(logFd) immediately after child.unref() in success path, before console.log success message.

representative.fix: After deleting the stale lock, immediately try to acquire the lock (write with 'wx') instead of continuing the loop. Or use atomic operations (rename) for lock acquisition.
